documents.title: HIV Prevention Methods — NACA Guidelines 2025
documents.content:
HIV Prevention Methods

HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) can be prevented through several evidence-based strategies.

Condom Use: Correct and consistent use of male or female condoms during sexual intercourse is one of the most effective methods of preventing HIV transmission. When used correctly, condoms reduce the risk of HIV transmission by approximately 90-95%.

Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP): PrEP involves taking antiretroviral medication daily to prevent HIV infection in people who are HIV-negative but at substantial risk. PrEP is highly effective when taken consistently, reducing the risk of getting HIV from sex by about 99%. In Nigeria, PrEP is available through accredited healthcare facilities. The recommended PrEP regimen in Nigeria is Tenofovir/Emtricitabine (TDF/FTC) taken as one tablet daily.

Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP): PEP is a course of antiretroviral medicines taken after potential exposure to HIV to prevent infection. PEP must be started within 72 hours of exposure and taken for 28 days. PEP is available at emergency departments and HIV treatment centres across Nigeria.

Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission (PMTCT): HIV-positive pregnant women can prevent transmission to their babies through antiretroviral therapy during pregnancy, safe delivery practices, and appropriate infant feeding counselling. With proper PMTCT, the risk of transmission can be reduced to less than 2%.

Voluntary Medical Male Circumcision (VMMC): Medical male circumcision reduces the risk of female-to-male HIV transmission by approximately 60%. VMMC is recommended by the World Health Organization as an additional HIV prevention strategy.

documents.title: ART Treatment Guidelines — Nigeria National Protocol 2025
documents.content:
Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) Treatment Guidelines

Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is the treatment of HIV infection with a combination of antiretroviral drugs. ART does not cure HIV but controls viral replication, allowing the immune system to recover and preventing progression to AIDS.

When to Start: Nigeria follows the WHO recommendation of treating all people living with HIV regardless of CD4 count (Test and Treat approach). ART should be initiated as soon as possible after diagnosis.

First-Line Regimen: The recommended first-line ART regimen for adults and adolescents in Nigeria is Tenofovir (TDF) + Lamivudine (3TC) + Dolutegravir (DTG), available as a fixed-dose combination taken as one tablet once daily. This regimen is preferred because of its high efficacy, good tolerability, high barrier to resistance, and convenience.

Adherence: Taking ART medication exactly as prescribed is critical. Missing doses can lead to drug resistance, treatment failure, and disease progression. Adherence of 95% or higher is recommended for optimal viral suppression. Patients should take their medication at the same time every day.

Missed Doses: If a dose is missed, it should be taken as soon as remembered on the same day. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with the regular schedule. Never take a double dose.

Side Effects: Common side effects of first-line ART include nausea, headache, fatigue, and dizziness, which usually improve within the first few weeks. Patients experiencing persistent or severe side effects should consult their healthcare provider rather than stopping medication.

Viral Load Monitoring: Viral load testing is the recommended approach to monitor ART response. The goal is to achieve an undetectable viral load (below 50 copies/ml) within 6 months of starting treatment. Undetectable = Untransmittable (U=U): a person with an undetectable viral load cannot transmit HIV sexually.

documents.title: HIV Testing Services — NACA Information Sheet
documents.content:
HIV Testing Services (HTS)

HIV testing is the only way to know your HIV status. Testing is voluntary, confidential, and available at no cost at public health facilities across Nigeria.

Types of Tests: Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) provide results within 15-20 minutes using a small blood sample from a finger prick. All positive rapid test results are confirmed with a second test using a different testing method.

Self-Testing: HIV self-test kits are available in Nigeria, allowing individuals to test themselves privately. A reactive (positive) self-test result should always be confirmed at a health facility.

Who Should Get Tested: Everyone aged 15 and above should know their HIV status. Testing is especially recommended for people with multiple sexual partners, people who have had unprotected sex, pregnant women, people with sexually transmitted infections, and anyone who has been exposed to HIV.

Window Period: The window period is the time between potential exposure to HIV and when a test can reliably detect the infection. For most rapid tests, the window period is 3-12 weeks. A negative test during the window period should be repeated after 3 months.

Testing is Confidential: All HIV testing in Nigeria is confidential. Your test results will not be shared with anyone without your explicit consent. No one can force you to take an HIV test.

documents.title: Common HIV Myths and Facts — NACA Communications
documents.content:
Common HIV Myths and Facts

Myth: HIV can be transmitted through mosquito bites.
Fact: HIV cannot be transmitted through mosquito bites, insect bites, or any other insect. HIV does not survive or replicate inside insects.

Myth: You can tell if someone has HIV by looking at them.
Fact: HIV has no visible symptoms in early stages. Many people living with HIV look and feel healthy for years. The only way to know your status is through testing.

Myth: HIV can be cured by traditional or herbal medicine.
Fact: There is currently no cure for HIV. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) effectively controls the virus but does not eliminate it. Claims of herbal or traditional cures for HIV are false and dangerous, as they may lead people to stop taking their ART medication.

Myth: HIV can be transmitted by sharing food, water, or utensils.
Fact: HIV cannot be transmitted through casual contact, sharing food, water, cups, plates, or utensils. HIV is not spread through saliva, sweat, or tears.

Myth: HIV can be spread through kissing.
Fact: HIV is not transmitted through closed-mouth kissing. There is an extremely small theoretical risk with deep open-mouth kissing if both partners have sores or bleeding gums, but no cases of transmission through kissing have been documented.

Myth: Only certain types of people get HIV.
Fact: HIV does not discriminate. Anyone can get HIV regardless of age, gender, sexual orientation, religion, or social status. HIV is transmitted through specific body fluids: blood, semen, vaginal fluids, rectal fluids, and breast milk.

Myth: If both partners have HIV, they don't need to use condoms.
Fact: Even if both partners are HIV-positive, condom use is still recommended to prevent reinfection with a different strain of HIV (superinfection) and to prevent other sexually transmitted infections.

documents.title: Crisis Support Resources — NACA Mental Health Guide
documents.content:
Crisis Support and Mental Health Resources

Receiving an HIV diagnosis or living with HIV can be emotionally challenging. It is normal to experience a range of emotions including fear, anger, sadness, or confusion. Support is available.

Immediate Support: If you are in crisis or having thoughts of self-harm, please reach out to a trained support agent through this chatbot by typing 'agent' or 'help'. You will be connected to a counsellor who can provide immediate support.

Counselling Services: Many HIV treatment centres in Nigeria offer free counselling services. These services are confidential and provided by trained counsellors who understand HIV-related issues.

Support Groups: Connecting with other people living with HIV through support groups can provide emotional support, practical advice, and reduce feelings of isolation. Ask your healthcare provider about support groups in your area.

Discrimination and Stigma: If you experience discrimination related to your HIV status, you have legal protections under Nigerian law. The HIV/AIDS Anti-Discrimination Act 2014 protects the rights of people living with HIV.

Remember: An HIV diagnosis is not a death sentence. With proper treatment and care, people living with HIV can live long, healthy, and fulfilling lives.

documents.title: HIV Testing and Diagnosis in Nigeria — NACA Aligned Knowledge Base 2026
documents.content:
HIV Testing and Diagnosis in Nigeria

Overview: In Nigeria, HIV testing services should follow the 5 Cs: consent, confidentiality, counselling, correct results, and connection or linkage to prevention, treatment, and care. HIV testing is the only reliable way to know a person's status.

Testing Options in Nigeria:
1. Facility based HIV testing services are available through public hospitals, primary health centres, antenatal clinics, TB clinics, STI clinics, private hospitals, and other approved service points.
2. Community based testing may be offered through mobile outreach, community distributors, one stop shops, and targeted services for priority populations.
3. HIV self testing is an approved additional approach in Nigeria. People may use oral fluid or blood based rapid diagnostic self tests in a private setting, but any reactive self test result must be confirmed at an approved health facility.
4. Pharmacies, Patent and Proprietary Medicine Vendors, and other designated outlets may serve as access points for HIV self test kits in Nigeria.

How HIV Self Testing Works:
1. The user collects their own specimen, follows the kit instructions, reads the result, and then seeks follow up services.
2. A non reactive self test does not rule out very recent infection during the window period.
3. A reactive self test is not a final diagnosis until confirmatory testing is done at a health facility.
4. Invalid results should be repeated with a new kit or followed by facility based testing.

Window Period:
1. The window period is the time between HIV exposure and when a test can detect infection.
2. Antibody based rapid tests may miss very early infection, especially in the first few weeks after exposure.
3. If exposure was recent and the first result is negative, repeat testing is advised according to national guidance and clinical assessment.
4. For a person with exposure in the last 72 hours, urgent assessment for PEP is more important than waiting for symptoms.

Who Should Be Encouraged to Test:
1. Anyone who does not know their HIV status.
2. Sexual partners of people living with HIV.
3. Pregnant women and breastfeeding women.
4. People with STIs, TB, recurrent infections, or recent high risk exposure.
5. People from priority or underserved populations who may not routinely use facility based services.

Where to Get Tested in Nigeria:
1. Public ART and HIV treatment centres.
2. Government and private hospitals offering HTS.
3. Primary health centres and antenatal care clinics.
4. Mobile HTS centres, voluntary counselling and testing centres, one stop shops, community distributors, pharmacies, and designated patent medicine outlets for self testing.

Important Safeguards:
1. HIV testing in Nigeria should be voluntary and based on informed consent except where specific lawful public health procedures apply.
2. Results should be kept confidential.
3. Positive diagnoses should be linked quickly to ART, counselling, partner services, and prevention support.
4. People should not be forced to test as a condition for employment or access to services.

documents.title: HIV Prevention and Risk Reduction in Nigeria — NACA Aligned Knowledge Base 2026
documents.content:
HIV Prevention and Risk Reduction in Nigeria

Overview: HIV prevention in Nigeria should be delivered as a combination package. No single method is perfect on its own. Risk reduction should be practical, non judgmental, and tailored to the person's situation.

Core Prevention Methods:
1. Correct and consistent condom use during vaginal or anal sex reduces HIV transmission risk and also helps prevent other sexually transmitted infections.
2. HIV testing for individuals and couples helps guide prevention decisions.
3. PrEP is for HIV negative people at substantial risk of HIV.
4. PEP is an emergency option after possible exposure and should be started as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 72 hours.
5. Viral suppression on ART prevents sexual transmission of HIV.
6. PMTCT services reduce the risk of transmission during pregnancy, delivery, and breastfeeding.

Condom Guidance:
1. Use a new condom for each act of sex.
2. Check expiry date and package integrity.
3. Use water based or silicone based lubricants with latex condoms where appropriate.
4. Do not use oil based products with latex condoms.
5. Condoms should be promoted without blame or shame.

PrEP in Nigeria:
1. Daily oral TDF based PrEP is part of HIV prevention programming for people at substantial risk.
2. A person should have an HIV negative test before starting PrEP and should return for follow up HIV testing and clinical review while using it.
3. PrEP protects against HIV but does not prevent pregnancy or all STIs, so condoms may still be recommended.
4. PrEP may be especially relevant for serodifferent couples, people with repeated high risk exposure, and some key and priority populations, based on assessment and national service availability.

PEP in Nigeria:
1. PEP is for emergency use after sexual exposure, needle stick injury, rape or sexual assault, or other significant contact with potentially infectious body fluids.
2. It should be started urgently and taken for 28 days.
3. Baseline HIV testing is needed, with follow up testing according to clinical guidance.
4. PEP is not a substitute for routine prevention planning if exposures are repeated.

Risk Assessment Topics for Counselling:
1. Type of exposure, when it occurred, and whether it happened within 72 hours.
2. Known HIV status and treatment status of the source partner if available.
3. Condom use, condom breakage, or no protection.
4. Presence of STIs, genital ulcers, or bleeding.
5. Pregnancy, breastfeeding, or recent sexual violence.
6. Need for PrEP, PEP, STI care, contraception, or psychosocial support.

Practical Risk Reduction Messages:
1. Know your status and encourage partner testing.
2. Use condoms correctly and consistently.
3. Seek PEP immediately after possible exposure.
4. Consider PrEP if risk is ongoing.
5. Do not share needles or sharp instruments.
6. Link pregnant women early to antenatal and PMTCT services.
7. Avoid myths, fear, and stigma driven decisions.

documents.title: Treatment and Living with HIV in Nigeria — NACA Aligned Knowledge Base 2026
documents.content:
Treatment and Living with HIV in Nigeria

Overview: HIV treatment in Nigeria follows the test and treat approach. A person diagnosed with HIV should be linked to care quickly and started on antiretroviral therapy as soon as clinically appropriate.

ART Basics:
1. ART does not cure HIV, but it suppresses the virus, protects the immune system, reduces illness, and helps people live long and productive lives.
2. Nigeria's treatment programme uses WHO aligned regimens, with dolutegravir based treatment widely adopted as the preferred standard first line approach for many adults and adolescents.
3. Treatment should be taken exactly as prescribed.

Adherence:
1. Good adherence means taking medicines every day as directed.
2. Poor adherence can lead to viral rebound, illness, and drug resistance.
3. Adherence support may include counselling, reminder systems, peer support, refill planning, and help with transport or stigma related barriers.
4. If a dose is missed, the person should follow the advice given by the treatment team and should not routinely double the next dose.

Viral Load and Viral Suppression:
1. Viral load is the main tool for monitoring treatment response in Nigeria.
2. When viral load becomes suppressed to very low or undetectable levels and stays there with good adherence, sexual transmission does not occur. This is the basis of U equals U, undetectable equals untransmittable.
3. Viral suppression takes time and requires regular treatment, follow up, and monitoring.
4. A person should not stop ART just because they feel well.

Long Term Care:
1. HIV care includes clinic follow up, viral load monitoring, adherence support, screening for TB and other infections, sexual and reproductive health support, and mental health support.
2. Pregnant women living with HIV need integrated PMTCT and maternal care.
3. Children, adolescents, and older adults may need tailored counselling and follow up.
4. People living with HIV can work, study, marry, have children, and plan for the future with proper care.

When to Seek Extra Clinical Review:
1. Persistent side effects.
2. Difficulty taking medicines regularly.
3. Symptoms of TB, weight loss, chronic diarrhoea, severe headache, or recurrent infections.
4. Pregnancy, breastfeeding, or drug interaction concerns.
5. Missed appointments or running low on medicines.

Key Reassurance Messages:
1. HIV is a manageable chronic condition with treatment.
2. Early diagnosis and early treatment improve outcomes.
3. Staying in care is just as important as starting care.
4. People living with HIV deserve dignity, privacy, and full access to healthcare.

documents.title: HIV Myths and Facts in Nigeria — NACA Aligned Knowledge Base 2026
documents.content:
HIV Myths and Facts in Nigeria

Purpose: This section corrects common myths, fear based beliefs, and culturally rooted misconceptions that may delay testing, treatment, or prevention.

Myth: HIV can be caught through handshakes, hugging, sharing toilets, sharing plates, or living in the same house.
Fact: HIV is not spread through casual contact, shared toilets, shared utensils, sweat, or tears.

Myth: Mosquitoes or other insects spread HIV.
Fact: HIV is not transmitted by mosquitoes or other insects.

Myth: You can know who has HIV by looking at them.
Fact: A person may look completely healthy and still have HIV. Testing is the only way to know.

Myth: Prayer, herbs, or traditional remedies can cure HIV.
Fact: There is no proven cure for HIV. ART is the evidence based treatment that controls the virus. People should not stop their medicines for unproven remedies.

Myth: HIV only affects certain groups or immoral people.
Fact: HIV can affect anyone. Risk depends on exposure, not on moral judgment, tribe, religion, or social class.

Myth: If both partners have HIV, condoms are no longer useful.
Fact: Condoms may still help prevent other STIs and may reduce the risk of superinfection with a different HIV strain.

Myth: A negative test immediately after exposure means there is definitely no HIV.
Fact: Early testing may miss infection during the window period. Repeat testing or clinical follow up may be needed.

Myth: HIV self testing alone is enough to confirm diagnosis.
Fact: A reactive self test must be confirmed at a health facility before HIV is diagnosed.

Myth: Starting ART means life is over.
Fact: People on ART can live long, healthy, productive lives and can achieve viral suppression.

Myth: People living with HIV must be excluded from school, work, marriage, or healthcare.
Fact: Discrimination is wrong and unlawful. Nigerian law protects people living with HIV against HIV related discrimination and unlawful disclosure of status.

documents.title: Emotional Support and Counselling for HIV in Nigeria — NACA Aligned Knowledge Base 2026
documents.content:
Emotional Support and Counselling for HIV in Nigeria

Overview: Fear, shock, shame, denial, anger, or sadness after an HIV diagnosis are common. Support should be trauma informed, confidential, non judgmental, and linked to practical next steps.

Immediate Post Diagnosis Support:
1. Allow the person time to process the result.
2. Explain that HIV is treatable and that starting care early improves health outcomes.
3. Arrange prompt linkage to confirmatory testing where needed, ART services, and counselling.
4. Screen for immediate safety concerns, including self harm risk, intimate partner violence, and homelessness.

Core Counselling Messages:
1. You are not alone.
2. HIV is not a moral failure.
3. Treatment works, and many people live long and fulfilling lives with HIV.
4. Your status is confidential and should not be disclosed unlawfully.
5. Support is available through health workers, counsellors, peer groups, and trusted community services.

Stigma Management in Nigeria:
1. Stigma may come from family, workplace, school, healthcare settings, or community beliefs.
2. Counselling should include practical disclosure planning, rights awareness, and safety planning.
3. People living with HIV in Nigeria are protected under the HIV and AIDS Anti Discrimination Act, 2014.
4. Unlawful disclosure of HIV status and discrimination in services or employment should be taken seriously.

Support Needs That May Be Assessed:
1. Need for partner or family disclosure support.
2. Anxiety, depression, sleep problems, or hopelessness.
3. Barriers to treatment such as transport, cost, work schedule, stigma, or domestic conflict.
4. Need for peer support groups, adolescent friendly services, or gender based violence support.

Reassurance for Chatbot Responses:
1. Encourage calm, not panic.
2. Give one clear next step at a time.
3. Avoid blame based language.
4. Offer referral to a trained provider or counsellor for crisis issues.
5. In emergencies, advise urgent in person help at the nearest health facility or emergency service.

Rights Based Messages:
1. HIV testing should be confidential.
2. No one should be forced to disclose status outside lawful clinical care processes.
3. Employment, education, and access to services should not be denied because of HIV status.
4. People living with HIV deserve dignity, privacy, and equal opportunity.
